10. Comparability Over Time and Space

BATS, ESTOC, HOT, and CARIACO each use different methods to determine pH, but each individual sampling program uses well-established methods that are consistent over time.

GCMs inherently use consistent algorithms over time and space.

The observed and projected time series cover the same four locations. Observed and projected series reflect the same indicator definition, although the former is naturally derived from station data while the latter is derived from a grid.

11. Data Limitations

The technical documentation for the Ocean Acidity indicator identifies some factors that may impact the confidence, application, or conclusions that readers can draw from the observed portion of this pairing. The documentation acknowledges that ocean chemistry is not uniform throughout the world’s oceans, and each of the four monitoring sites is subject to different local influences. It also notes that changes in ocean pH and mineral saturation caused by the uptake of atmospheric carbon dioxide can take a long time to spread to deeper waters, so the full effect of current warming on ocean pH may not be seen for many decades, if not centuries.

Future projections of any variable have inherent uncertainty, as described in Section 12 below. Ocean acidity is influenced by multiple systems and processes, so it may be less direct to model than, say, surface air temperature.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. Details on uncertainty measurements can be found in the following documents and references therein: Bindoff et al. (2007), Bates et al. (2012), Dore et al. (2009), and González-Dávila et al. (2010).

Model outputs inevitably reflect model uncertainty. Each GCM represents aspects of, and processes within, the climate system differently. These differences will lead to differences in how the GCMs represent both present-day climate and how the climate responds to changes in greenhouse gases. For example, GCMs differ in climate sensitivity, defined as the increase in global temperature when carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubles relative to pre-industrial times. Even a single GCM will yield different results if presented with different initial conditions, as the chaotic processes within the model will lead to different timing of various modes of variability within the model (such as the El Niño cycle). The shaded bands in the graph for this pairing illustrate this type of uncertainty in the spread of models, as well as year-to-year variations due to internal variability within each model.

Interpreting projections also requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents four widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

13. Sources of Variability

The pH is a property of seawater that can vary with temperature and salinity. Therefore, it can vary naturally over space and time. Variability in ocean surface pH data has been associated with regional changes in the natural carbon cycle influenced by changes in ocean circulation, climate variability (seasonal changes), and biological activity (Bindoff et al., 2007).

The construction of this pairing addresses variability in a few ways:

  • Selecting four locations in different parts of the world’s oceans, rather than relying on a single station.
  • Acknowledging monthly-scale variability by showing it in the graphs.
  • Smoothing the central seven GCM estimates with an 11-year moving average.
